title: Spring Lecture #37: Security Authentication Internals
sources: code/springPracticalDemo (SecurityConfig, CustomUserDetails, CustomUserDetailsService, AuthService, UserRepository, RoleController)

questions.question: What is the job of `DelegatingFilterProxy` in Spring Security's servlet architecture?
options: It checks the username and password against the database
It decides which URL patterns require the ADMIN role
It is a servlet filter registered with the container (e.g. Tomcat) that delegates the request to Spring-managed filter beans such as `FilterChainProxy`
It replaces the `DispatcherServlet` so that controllers receive only authenticated requests
questions.explanation: `DelegatingFilterProxy` bridges the servlet container's lifecycle and Spring's `ApplicationContext`: the container knows it as an ordinary filter, and it forwards the work to a Spring bean, normally `FilterChainProxy`. Password checks happen in authentication providers and access rules in the authorization filter; the `DispatcherServlet` still runs afterwards.

questions.question: Your app logs users in with their email address, but `UserDetailsService` only has `loadUserByUsername(String username)`. What is the correct approach?
options: Implement `loadUserByUsername` so that it looks the user up by email (e.g. `userRepository.findByEmail(...)`) and returns a `UserDetails`
Rename the `email` column to `username`, because Spring Security queries that column directly
Create a second interface `UserDetailsByEmailService`, which Spring Security detects automatically
Email login is impossible with `DaoAuthenticationProvider`; a custom filter is required
questions.explanation: The method name is historical: its argument is just the login identifier the user typed. The notes show the same contract implemented with `findByEmail(email)`. Spring Security never queries your columns itself; it only calls your `UserDetailsService`.
questions.source: notes p16-18 (CustomUserDetailsService, email as login identity)

questions.question: This is the application's only `SecurityFilterChain` bean. `HomeController` maps `GET /home` with no security annotations. What happens for `GET /home` sent without any credentials?
options: 401, because `anyRequest().authenticated()` covers every URL in the application
200: no `SecurityFilterChain` matches `/home`, so no Spring Security filters run for it and the controller is reached
403, because unmatched requests are denied by default
Spring Boot adds its default chain for `/home`, so the browser is redirected to `/login`
questions.explanation: `securityMatcher("/api/**")` limits the whole chain, including its `anyRequest()` rule, to `/api/**` requests. Because a custom `SecurityFilterChain` exists, Boot's default chain backs off, so `/home` matches no chain and is not protected. That is why the notes recommend a general fallback chain ordered last.
questions.source: notes p4-6 (Request matching, first matching chain wins, fallback chain)

questions.question: `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter` is part of the chain. What does it do when an already-logged-in browser sends `GET /courses`?
options: It re-reads the password from the session and authenticates again on every request
It queries the database to refresh the user's roles before each request
It rejects the request, because it only allows `POST /login`
It sees that this is not a form-login request (such as `POST /login`) and simply continues the chain
questions.explanation: An authentication filter first checks whether the request contains the mechanism it understands; for form login that is the login-processing request. Other requests pass through with `chain.doFilter(...)`. Even on a login request the filter only extracts credentials and calls the `AuthenticationManager`; it does no database work itself.
questions.source: notes p7-10 (A filter does not authenticate every request)

questions.question: An admin creates a role through the lecture's `POST /api/roles` with body `{"name":"ADMIN"}` and assigns it to Aditya. The security config contains `.requestMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")`. Aditya calls `GET /admin/stats` with correct HTTP Basic credentials. What is the result?
options: 200, because `hasRole("ADMIN")` matches an authority named `ADMIN`
401, because the role name is not a valid authority, so login fails
403: Aditya authenticates, but his authority is `ADMIN` while `hasRole("ADMIN")` requires the authority `ROLE_ADMIN`
500, because `SimpleGrantedAuthority` rejects names without the `ROLE_` prefix
questions.explanation: The adapter turns each role name into an authority unchanged, so Aditya gets `ADMIN`. `hasRole("ADMIN")` checks for `ROLE_ADMIN`, which is why the lecture stores role names as `ROLE_USER` / `ROLE_ADMIN`. Authentication succeeds (correct password), so this is an authorization failure: 403, not 401.
questions.source: code: CustomUserDetails.getAuthorities, RoleController; notes p30 (Role names, hasRole)

questions.question: Support sets `enabled = false` for Rohit in the `users` table. Rohit then calls `GET /api/users/hello` with HTTP Basic and his correct password. What happens?
options: 200, because the password matches and `enabled` is only checked at registration
Authentication fails (401) because `DaoAuthenticationProvider` checks the account state exposed by `CustomUserDetails.isEnabled()`, so no authenticated result reaches the `SecurityContext`
403, because a disabled user is authenticated but has no authorities
The request succeeds once, then the session is invalidated
questions.explanation: Database authentication is more than password comparison: the provider also checks `isEnabled()`, `isAccountNonLocked()` and the expiry flags from `UserDetails`. A disabled account fails authentication even with the right password, so the request is treated as unauthenticated (401) and never reaches the controller.
questions.source: notes p21-22 (Step 6: account status), p40 (Disable the account demo); code: CustomUserDetails.isEnabled

questions.question: During an HTTP Basic login in the lecture app, which component actually calls `passwordEncoder.matches(raw, stored)`?
options: `DaoAuthenticationProvider`, after `ProviderManager` selects it because it supports `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken` and it has loaded the user via `CustomUserDetailsService`
`BasicAuthenticationFilter`, right after decoding the Base64 header
`CustomUserDetailsService.loadUserByUsername`, before returning the `UserDetails`
`ProviderManager` itself, which compares passwords for all providers
questions.explanation: The filter only extracts credentials and builds an unauthenticated token; `ProviderManager` (the usual `AuthenticationManager`) delegates to a provider that supports that token type. `DaoAuthenticationProvider` loads the user via the `UserDetailsService` (which just finds the user) and then verifies the password with the configured `PasswordEncoder`.
questions.source: notes p9-12, p18-23 (Complete internal login flow)

questions.question: The application is started against a brand-new database (the `role` table is empty). A client calls `POST /api/users/register` with `{"username":"aditya","password":"secret123"}`. What happens, given the lecture's `register` method?
options: The user is saved without any role and can log in but access nothing
Hibernate creates the missing `ROLE_USER` row automatically because of `@ManyToMany`
The user is saved first, then the request fails while adding the role
`Optional.get()` throws `NoSuchElementException` before `save()`, so the request fails with a server error and no user is stored
questions.explanation: `findByName` returns an empty Optional, and `get()` throws before `userRepository.save(user)` is reached. `@ManyToMany` without cascade never creates Role rows. That is why the notes' demo sequence starts with 'Create the default role' and their version uses `orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalStateException("ROLE_USER not found"))` for a clearer error.
questions.source: code: AuthService.register; notes p27, p35-36, p39 (default role, demonstration sequence)

questions.question: The lecture's `UserRepository` declares `@EntityGraph(attributePaths = "roles") Optional<User> findByUsername(String username);`. A teammate removes the `@EntityGraph` as 'unnecessary'. `User.roles` is a plain `@ManyToMany` and `loadUserByUsername` is not `@Transactional`. What is the most likely result at login?
options: Nothing changes, because `@ManyToMany` is EAGER by default
Login fails with a `LazyInitializationException` when `getAuthorities()` reads `user.getRoles()` after the repository call's persistence context has closed
Login succeeds, but the user gets no authorities, because lazy collections return empty lists when not loaded
The query fails at startup, because derived queries require an entity graph for collections
questions.explanation: `@ManyToMany` is LAZY by default (lecture #31). Authentication runs in the security filter chain, before the web layer's open-session support, so after `findByUsername` returns, the `User` is detached. When `DaoAuthenticationProvider` builds the result it calls `getAuthorities()`, which touches the uninitialized `roles` collection and fails. The entity graph fetches roles in the same query.
questions.source: code: UserRepository.java, CustomUserDetails.getAuthorities; day 31 notes (default fetch types)

questions.question: The lecture's `CustomUserDetailsService` throws `UsernameNotFoundException("User Not found")` for an unknown username. With the default `DaoAuthenticationProvider` settings, how does the HTTP Basic client experience an unknown username compared with a wrong password?
options: Both get the same 401 response: by default the provider hides `UsernameNotFoundException` as a `BadCredentialsException`, so the response does not reveal whether the account exists
Unknown user gets 404, wrong password gets 401
Unknown user gets a 500 error because the exception is unchecked; wrong password gets 401
Unknown user gets a 401 whose body says "User Not found"; wrong password gets "Bad credentials"
questions.explanation: `DaoAuthenticationProvider` (through `AbstractUserDetailsAuthenticationProvider`'s default `hideUserNotFoundExceptions = true`) converts a not-found user into `BadCredentialsException`, so both failures look the same to the client. This is the framework doing what lecture #35 recommended manually: don't reveal unnecessary failure details. No trusted authentication is placed in the context in either case.
questions.source: notes p24-25 (What happens when authentication fails); code: CustomUserDetailsService
